title: CAT: turn a mock into better VARC, DILR and QA decisions
description: Review CAT passages, set selection and quantitative errors using original worked checks, a repeatable mock audit and a practical final-weeks routine.
intro: More mocks help only if they change your next decision. This guide focuses on evidence in VARC, set selection in DILR and setup accuracy in QA. The official CAT portal lists admit-card downloads from 4 November and the test on 29 November 2026; those are scheduled dates, not a release claim.

sections.title: Audit decisions before the headline percentile
sections.body:
Save a mock log with three fields for each problem: what you tried, why you chose it and where the reasoning failed. Review correct guesses too. A lucky option can conceal the same gap that causes tomorrow's wrong answer.

Separate a learning error from a selection error. If a question remains difficult without a timer, repair the concept. If you solve it cleanly later, inspect why another question consumed its time. Mock percentiles depend on that provider's participant pool; they are not official CAT percentiles or admission probabilities. Use score trends under similar conditions rather than one dramatic result.

sections.title: VARC: attach each answer to evidence
sections.body:
For a passage, write a one-sentence claim and a short note about each paragraph's role. Test close options against the text. Reject an option that turns “some” into “all” or an observed association into a proven cause.

For inference, choose the smallest conclusion the passage supports. Do not reward an option just because it sounds knowledgeable. Review the [original comprehension exercise](/study-guides/reading-comprehension-find-evidence/) and then apply its evidence-line method to a longer passage. Record whether an error came from scope, tone, attribution or a missed qualification.

sections.title: DILR: decide whether a set is becoming solvable
sections.body:
Before building a large table, identify the entities, constraints and question demands. Start with the strongest fixed information. Recheck whether a condition applies to all cases or only one subgroup; a silent assumption can invalidate every later answer.

During review, try a second representation: a grid, a timeline, cases or a simple equation. Count how much useful information you gained before deciding to continue or leave. This is a decision practice, not a universal minute limit for every candidate. A set you did not select can be valuable homework if it teaches a more economical representation.

sections.title: QA: repair setup and check answer conditions
sections.body:
Write variables and units before using a shortcut. Check whether a ratio, percentage base or average refers to the same group throughout the problem. After solving, test sign, range, integrality and any conditions stated in the question.

Use a mixed arithmetic block, then a targeted block for the concept that failed. Keep accuracy separate from attempt count. Confirm the current CAT bulletin and on-screen instructions for question types and marking rather than applying a coaching rule to every item. The [CAT score tool](/exams/cat/score-calculator/) is a calculation aid, not a promise of percentile or college admission.

sections.title: Protect the last weeks from unfocused expansion
sections.body:
Alternate a full mock review with smaller skill blocks. Leave room for rest and a realistic exam-day routine. Do not replace the whole plan because one mock score fell; inspect whether the cause was concept, decisions or conditions first.

Check the [CAT dates](/exams/cat/calendar/) and official portal for the actual admit-card release. Read your own reporting time, test city and permitted documents when available. The closed October edit window is separate from admit-card downloads. Application discrepancies should go through the official helpdesk rather than a guessed correction link.

drills.prompt: An author says a six-week trial increased visits but does not isolate the cause. Can you infer that one change alone caused the increase?
drills.explanation: The inference adds causal certainty that the stated evidence does not provide. Preserve the author’s limitation.

drills.prompt: A group has 12 people averaging 70. Three more averaging 80 join. What is the new average?
drills.explanation: The combined total is 12 × 70 + 3 × 80 = 1080. Divide by 15, not by the number of groups: 1080/15 = 72.

checklist: Log why I chose each attempted problem.
Review correct guesses as well as errors.
Map one VARC passage to evidence.
Retry one DILR set with a better representation.
Repair one QA setup error and check official admission instructions.

sources.label: Official CAT portal and information bulletin

faqs.q: Does a mock percentile equal the CAT percentile?
faqs.a: No. The participant pool, paper and scoring context differ.

faqs.q: Are CAT admit cards already released by this guide?
faqs.a: No release is claimed. The official portal schedules downloads from 4 November; check it for actual availability.
